definition.text: The scarcity rent on a finite resource: the extra value it earns because extracting it today leaves less for the future.

facts.text: It is the maximum rent obtainable while emptying the resource stock, also called scarcity or depletion rent.
Under Hotelling's rule it rises each year at the rate of interest, reflecting growing scarcity.
It reflects choice over time: if today's price were lower, a producer would rather extract less now and more later.
Scarcity rents help explain why the best tax on a pollutant from a finite fuel can be lower than the pollutant's marginal damages.

definition.text: The tendency for extraction to become costlier as a resource stock is drawn down, pushing producers to less accessible sites and lower-grade ores.

facts.text: Because ores are concentrated unevenly, mining eventually meets diminishing returns, and extraction costs and prices of extra output tend to rise over time.
Falling average ore grades mean deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock.
Even with constant extraction costs, a resource's value rises as it grows scarcer.

title: Resource scarcity indicators

definition.text: Measures, such as a resource's inflation-adjusted price, used to judge whether natural resources are becoming scarcer.

facts.text: Because total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists do not see physical scarcity as a good indicator of availability.
An alternative view measures the usable quantity of a resource through its price and opportunity cost.
The Simon–Ehrlich wager used the inflation-adjusted prices of five metals as its agreed measure of scarcity.
From 2005 through 2013, real prices of energy and metals stayed well above their long-term averages.
